# Grading note — Sub-item 1b (−2 points if triggered)

This sub-item penalizes any discussion of implications for transaction types other than SCHEMA or ISSUER_KEY. Treat unnamed generalizations exactly the same as named other types: if the answer states or implies that the deepcopy behavior extends beyond the two in-scope types — even without naming a single other type — deduct the full 2 points. Sweeping phrasings such as "this applies to every transaction," "any reply's result is affected," "all ledger writes," "for all transaction types," or similar blanket claims count as asserting implications for other transaction types and trigger the deduction, because the generalization necessarily reaches types outside SCHEMA and ISSUER_KEY.

Do not deduct when the answer confines its discussion of the deepcopy's effects to SCHEMA and ISSUER_KEY transactions, including when it speaks generally about `result`, `reply.result`, or the serialization step but keeps the scope of the described behavior tied to those two types (e.g., by referring to the code path that handles SCHEMA and ISSUER_KEY). Discussion of the general mechanics of `deepcopy` itself — that it produces an independent copy so later mutation of `result` does not propagate — is not a generalization to other transaction types and is not deductible on its own; the deduction applies only when the answer asserts that the resulting behavior or implications hold for transactions beyond SCHEMA and ISSUER_KEY, whether those types are named or left unnamed.

**Grading note for sub-item 2a (data serialization reflected in the ledger):**

Deduct the point unless the answer makes an affirmative, ledger-specific claim that the serialized data ends up in the ledger, attributed to the post-deepcopy object, and set against a second, differently-served consumer.

Concretely, no deduction requires all of the following. First, the answer must name the ledger itself — "the ledger," "the ledger append," "the txn log," "the merkle tree," or the equivalent exact ledger mechanism. Generic persistence wording such as "the data is saved," "it is persisted," "it is stored in the database," or "it is sent downstream" does not satisfy the item and gets the deduction. Second, the claim must be affirmative about the ledger: an answer that only states the serialization is *not* reflected in the graph, leaving the ledger case to be inferred, or that says only "other consumers are unaffected except the graph," gets the deduction. Third, the answer must attribute the ledger's serialized content to the post-deepcopy object — `reply.result`, i.e. the copy the ledger receives. If it says the serialization reaches the ledger via the original `result` dict, or never identifies which object the ledger gets, deduct. Fourth, the answer must separate two distinct downstream consumers receiving different payloads (the serialized copy versus the unserialized original); if it names only one downstream use — only `storeTxnInGraph` / "the graph," or only "later operations" — or speaks generically of "storage operations" without saying which consumer gets the serialized version and which gets the original, deduct.

Where these four conditions are met, do not deduct for imprecise or hedged phrasing: the item asks only whether the ledger is discussed as a consumer of the serialized data, so wording that is tentative or partially loose still counts as "mentioned."

An answer that does raise the ledger as a consumer of the serialized data — and so counts as "mentioned" under 2a_accuracy_of_the_claim (no deduct) — but credits the serialization to the original `result` dict (or names no object), or names the ledger as the only downstream consumer with no contrasting second consumer, must be deducted under the other two forks. **Sub-item 2b — "the data serialization will not be reflected in the graph" (1 point deduction if not mentioned):**

Award no deduction whenever the answer addresses, in any form, what the graph receives with respect to the serialized data. This sub-item tests only that the graph's handling of the data is discussed at all, not the precision or even the factual correctness of the claim. A single clause is enough — the deduction trigger is "if this is not mentioned," so a bare assertion such as "so the graph stores the unserialized data" fully satisfies it; no extended discussion of the consequence is required. The exact words "serialization is not reflected in the graph" are likewise unnecessary: it suffices that the fact follows from what is said, e.g. "deepcopy keeps the original `result` intact so the graph gets the unmodified dict," or "`reply.result` still holds the dict form when it is stored in the graph." Even an answer that gets the direction wrong — e.g. claiming the graph also stores the serialized data — should not be deducted here, since it has explicitly addressed the graph's relationship to the data serialization.

Deduct the point only when neither an explicit statement nor a direct implication about what the graph receives with respect to the serialized data is present anywhere in the answer — that is, when the graph's relationship to the serialized/unserialized data is never addressed at all.
